question: Can separating the learning rates of a two-layer network's outer weights and inner neuron positions yield finite-width global convergence in a feature-learning regime?

key_findings.claim: For a one-dimensional shallow network with smoothed-step activations and a piecewise-constant target, the paper proves high-probability convergence of gradient flow to arbitrarily small loss with a fixed finite number of neurons.
key_findings.evidence: The main theorem requires sufficiently many uniformly initialized neuron positions, small activation smoothing and a small inner-to-outer learning-rate ratio; unlike NTK or mean-field proofs, width is not sent to infinity.

key_findings.claim: In the singular two-timescale limit, outer weights rapidly track their least-squares optimum while only neurons adjacent to target discontinuities move, reducing feature learning to an analyzable slow positional flow.
key_findings.evidence: The best piecewise-constant approximation has zero coefficients away from discontinuities; a local race aligns selected neuron positions to jumps while preserving separation conditions.

key_findings.claim: Simulations reproduce the predicted alignment only in sufficiently separated timescales; standard-timescale runs can create neuron-free gaps, while finite-step SGD stabilizes at nonzero approximation error.
key_findings.evidence: The numerical section compares gradient flow and SGD across epsilon and activation smoothing, shows a failure at epsilon=1, and notes the very small inner updates can require hundreds of millions of steps.

anchors.section: Failure outside the two-timescale regime and discussion

method.core_idea: Make feature learning provable by optimizing linear outer coefficients much faster than nonlinear neuron positions and applying singular-perturbation analysis.
method.mechanism: Solve the outer least-squares problem conditionally on positions, analyze the induced slow position flow in the zero-smoothing/timescale limit, prove favorable random initialization geometry, then bound deviations for positive smoothing and timescale ratio.
assumptions: Inputs are one-dimensional and the target is piecewise constant with separated jumps and bounded values.
Hidden units are translated smoothed steps with no learned input slopes.
Outer and inner layers use an extremely separated learning-rate ratio and full-batch gradient flow.

techniques.role: Eliminates fast outer weights through their conditional least-squares optimum.
Tracks slow hidden positions toward target discontinuities.
Transfers convergence from the singular limit to small positive smoothing and timescale ratio.

evaluations.setting: One-dimensional piecewise-constant targets plus exploratory higher-dimensional and ReLU teacher simulations.
evaluations.metric: L2 loss, neuron locations, and convergence behavior versus timescale ratio and SGD steps.
evaluations.result: Small ratios exhibit alignment and lower error predicted by the theory; equal timescales can open empty regions and fail recovery, and tiny ratios train very slowly in raw steps.
evaluations.baseline: Standard equal-timescale training and the idealized two-timescale gradient-flow limit.

limitations: The theorem covers a specialized one-dimensional translated-step network and piecewise-constant target.
Gradient flow omits discretization and stochastic noise; the paper only sketches how SGD errors might be controlled.
The required timescale separation can make practical training extremely slow.
Exploratory ReLU and higher-dimensional experiments are outside the proved setting.
failure_modes: Too-large inner learning rates let neurons cluster and leave parts of the target uncovered.
Insufficient width or unfavorable initialization leaves a discontinuity without flanking neurons.
Positive activation smoothing creates irreducible approximation error for a discontinuous target.
reusable_insights: Analytically eliminating a linear parameter block can expose otherwise hidden feature dynamics.
Provable feature learning need not require infinite width, but finite-width results can demand highly structured targets and optimization schedules.
Iteration complexity must accompany continuous-time convergence when timescale ratios are extreme.
open_questions: Can comparable finite-width results handle learned slopes, ReLU networks, and multidimensional data?
Can adaptive schedules obtain the alignment benefit without extremely slow inner updates?
What stochastic-gradient noise levels preserve neuron coverage and convergence?

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: Principal infinite-width convergence framework contrasted by the target.
competitive_landscape.difference: NTK freezes features in the infinite-width limit; the target proves movement of a fixed finite set of neuron positions under separated timescales.

competitive_landscape.title: On the Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Over-parameterized Models using Optimal Transport
competitive_landscape.difference: The optimal-transport analysis evolves an infinite particle distribution; the target keeps finite width but imposes a one-dimensional step-function structure.

competitive_landscape.title: Ultra-fast feature learning for the training of two-layer neural networks in the two-timescale regime
competitive_landscape.relationship: Later direct extension of two-timescale/variable-projection feature learning.
competitive_landscape.difference: Barboni et al. analyze a mean-field teacher feature distribution and diffusion dynamics; the target gives an earlier finite-neuron discontinuity-alignment proof.

novelty_assessment: The central novelty is a finite-width global convergence proof in a genuine feature-learning regime through layerwise timescale separation. Its conceptual reach is broader than its theorem: the proof depends on a particularly tractable 1D step network, and practical iteration cost is a serious caveat.
reviewer_notes: Read all 34 extracted pages, including proofs and appendix experiments. The panel includes the principal frameworks contrasted in the paper and a later direct two-timescale development, checked on primary arXiv pages 2026-08-23.
